title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: For every positive integer $t$, if an $n$-vertex graph $G$ does not contain $K_{t+1}$ as a minor then $\alpha(G) \geq n/t$.
context_text: $\alpha(G)$ denotes the independence number. Since every $n$-vertex graph has chromatic number at least $\lceil n/\alpha(G)\rceil$, Hadwiger's conjecture (every graph with no $K_{t+1}$ minor is $t$-colourable) would imply this statement, which is therefore a natural weakening of it that has received a lot of attention (see Seymour's survey on Hadwiger's conjecture). Duchet and Meyniel proved in 1982 that the bound holds within a factor of $2$: every $n$-vertex graph with no $K_{t+1}$ minor has $\alpha(G)\ge\frac{n}{2t}+\frac{1}{2}$; Fox gave the first constant-factor improvement, $\alpha(G)\ge n/((2-c)t)$ with $c>0.017$, improved by Balogh and Kostochka to $c>1/19.2$. The present paper studies the conjecture for triangle-free graphs, proving that for every $0<\varepsilon<1/26$ and $t$ large enough every triangle-free $n$-vertex graph with no $K_t$ minor has $\alpha(G)\ge n/t^{1-\varepsilon}$, much more than the $\Omega(n\sqrt{\log t}/t)$ given by combining the Kostochka–Thomason average-degree bound with Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi.
notes: No explicit attribution appears in the conjecture header; the paper describes it as having 'received quite a lot of attention' and directs the reader to Seymour's survey [31], indicating it is a community/folklore conjecture rather than one originated by the paper authors. Classified as 'states' per the no-attribution-in-header rule.

title: Conjecture on $MR_t(s,k)$ for $s \geq 4$
statement_text: Fix an integer $s\geq 4$. Is it true that for every $0<\varepsilon<1/s$ there exists a positive integer $t_0$ such that for all $t\geq t_0$, if $G$ is a $K_s$-free graph without a $K_{t}$-minor, then $\alpha(G)\geq \frac{|G|}{t^{1-\varepsilon}}$? (In terms of $t$-minor Ramsey numbers: $MR_t(s,k)\le t^{1-\varepsilon}k$ for sufficiently large $t$; here $\varepsilon$ cannot be larger than $1/s$.)
context_text: $K_s$-free means having no $K_s$ subgraph (clique number less than $s$), and $\alpha(G)$ is the independence number. The $t$-minor Ramsey number $MR_t(s,k)$ is the smallest $n$ such that every $K_t$-minor-free graph on $n$ vertices contains a copy of $K_s$ or an independent set of size $k$; it generalises the planar Ramsey numbers of Walker and of Steinberg and Tovey, which grow linearly. The authors' main theorem is the case $s=3$: for every $0<\varepsilon<1/26$ there is $t_0$ such that for all $t\ge t_0$ every triangle-free $n$-vertex graph with no $K_t$ minor has $\alpha(G)\ge n/t^{1-\varepsilon}$, i.e. $MR_t(3,k)\le t^{1-\varepsilon}k$; by a random construction of Erdős this cannot hold beyond $\varepsilon=1/3$ (up to a logarithmic factor). For fixed $s\ge4$, the lower bounds on $R(s,k)$ of Bohman ($s=4$) and Bohman–Keevash ($s\ge5$) give graphs with no $K_s$ subgraph and no independent set of order $n^{2/(s+1)}$ up to polylogarithmic factors, which are $K_t$-minor-free for $t=n^{1-\frac{s-2}{s(s-1)-2}}$ and have no independent set of size $n/t^{1-\frac{1}{s}}$, so $\varepsilon<1/s$ is necessary; the authors nevertheless expect a result similar to the triangle-free case. A less ambitious goal is to answer the question for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, for some $\varepsilon_0>0$.
